title: How to Turn Customer Support Questions Into LinkedIn Posts
summary: Use recurring onboarding questions and support tickets to write useful LinkedIn posts. See how to turn one post-launch problem into a checklist.
body_markdown:
When customers ask the same support question after launch, there may be a lesson worth sharing. Look for the decision the team is stuck on, check the answer with the person who handles it, and turn it into a short LinkedIn post that helps readers make that decision. Use your own words and leave private ticket details out.


## Look for a handoff, not just a frequent ticket


Password resets can make up a lot of tickets without giving your audience much to think about. A smaller cluster may be more useful: three onboarding teams understand how to start a workflow, but none knows who handles an exception once it goes live. That points to a decision other operators may recognize.


In a weekly support review, ask which question required an explanation rather than a link to the docs. Write down the point where the customer got stuck, which role had to step in, and what would have made the handoff clearer. A few sentences from the person who handled it are enough. You don’t need to circulate recordings or copy tickets into a writing brief.


## Show readers the check they can run


Here’s a hypothetical example: a new workflow sends supplier requests to finance. When a request comes through without a purchase order, support tells the customer to ask finance. Finance assumes the operations team is already handling it. The team needs a clear way to route that exception.


A LinkedIn post could open with: “Before you hand off a new workflow, run one request that’s missing a required field. See where it lands and who picks it up.” Then give readers three things to check:


1. Name the operator who owns the exception after launch. Use a role, not “the team.”
2. Decide what that person can resolve and where they escalate the rest.
3. Run an example with the person on duty. Check that they get the alert, know what to do, and can tell when the issue is closed.


That’s the post. There’s no need to cast a customer as the hero or add an outcome you haven’t measured. The value is that a reader can run the same check on their own workflow.


## Keep the source notes out of the post


Give the writer the pattern and the approved explanation, not a ticket screenshot. Even without a company name, a combination of details such as industry, timing, and the tool involved can identify the customer. If the real story needs those details, ask for permission or use a clearly labeled hypothetical example.


Have the support or onboarding lead check the draft. Ask whether the steps still work for a reader using a different setup and whether a caveat is missing. If the same question keeps surfacing, consider improving the help article as well. The public post helps readers spot the problem; your documentation tells customers how to fix it in your product.


For related material from before the sale, see the[guide to turning sales objections into LinkedIn content](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/sales-objections-linkedin-content) . If you have permission and a measured result to share, use the[customer story guide](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/customer-story-linkedin-post) instead.


## Frequently asked questions


### Which support questions make good LinkedIn posts?


Choose questions that reveal a decision other teams face. Who owns an exception, when to escalate it, or what to check before launch are useful starting points. Skip account-specific troubleshooting unless there’s a broader lesson.


### Can I use a real support ticket as an example?


Use an aggregated pattern or a labeled hypothetical by default. Get permission before sharing a quote, screenshot, or identifiable incident, and follow any confidentiality commitments.


### How is this different from a customer story?


A customer story explains what happened to a specific customer and what changed. A support-based educational post gives readers a method they can use without claiming that a particular customer followed it or got a particular result.
